title: Rendering and Animation Optimization
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of Rendering and Animation Optimization and recognize when it is useful.
Apply a relevant property, selector, or technique from this lesson in a small stylesheet.
Inspect the browser result and explain one behavior, limitation, or compatibility consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore Rendering and Animation Optimization through a small CSS example, a visual guide, and one practical check. You do not need to memorize every property at once; focus on the decision the browser is making.
content.why_it_matters: Rendering and Animation Optimization helps you build interfaces that remain understandable, maintainable, and usable as content and viewport conditions change.

content_blocks.title: Motion lifecycle
content_blocks.alt_text: A motion effect should communicate a state, remain optional, and respect user preferences. Labels show the concept flow.
content_blocks.caption: Use the labeled steps as a reasoning guide; detailed behavior is described in the lesson.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Motion can communicate state and continuity, but it must remain subtle, performant, and optional. Prefer transform and opacity for many effects, honor `prefers-reduced-motion`, and avoid making essential content depend on animation.

content_blocks.title: A useful way to practice
content_blocks.text: Start with one element or component. Use the concepts in this lesson—transform and opacity animation patterns, understanding forced synchronous layout, will-change and its limitations—and change one declaration at a time. Compare the page before and after the change.

items.title: Transform and opacity animation patterns
items.text: Keep motion nonessential, honor reduced-motion preferences, and inspect performance on a real device when practical.

items.title: Understanding forced synchronous layout
items.text: Connect understanding forced synchronous layout to the main idea in rendering and animation optimization, then verify it in a minimal browser example.

items.title: will-change and its limitations
items.text: Connect will-change and its limitations to the main idea in rendering and animation optimization, then verify it in a minimal browser example.

items.title: Containment and content visibility
items.text: Make the query container explicit and keep base component styles useful before the condition becomes true.

items.title: Performance profiling in browser tools
items.text: Record the observation and environment, isolate the smallest cause, and repeat the same check after changing the rule.

content_blocks.expected_output: The card uses a small transform change and disables the transition for users who request reduced motion.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Put this snippet in styles.css and link it from a minimal index.html file with a viewport meta tag. Add elements whose classes match the selectors, open the page in a modern browser, and inspect computed styles. This lesson editor displays the expected result as a guide; it is not a server-side arbitrary-code runner.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original CSS snippet, save the file, and repeat the test. Remove temporary debugging rules before keeping a final version.

content_blocks.title: Keep in mind
content_blocks.text: Keep the effect brief and nonessential, and provide a reduced-motion alternative.

content.task: Try it yourself: build a small example that demonstrates Rendering and Animation Optimization. Use the simplest relevant selector and one or more declarations, inspect the browser result, and explain it in your own words.
task_acceptance_criteria: The stylesheet uses valid CSS syntax for the chosen feature.
The intended element or state visibly changes when the rule applies.
The behavior is checked with browser tools or a documented manual checklist.
hints: Write the smallest rule that can demonstrate the concept.
Inspect which element matched and which declaration won before adding more selectors.
For a developing or optional feature, check browser support and preserve a useful fallback.
content.expected_output: The card uses a small transform change and disables the transition for users who request reduced motion.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to connect a visual change to its cause.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one property, save, and compare again.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the last rule always wins.
common_mistakes.why: The cascade also considers origin, importance, layers and selector specificity; scope and source order may also matter.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect matched declarations and computed styles before changing the stylesheet.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only one viewport or interaction state.
common_mistakes.why: A rule can work at one width and fail when content, focus, zoom or preferences change.
common_mistakes.fix: Repeat the check at narrow and wide widths and include keyboard focus or reduced-motion checks when relevant.

summary: Rendering and Animation Optimization is easiest to learn by connecting syntax to a rendered result.
Keep selectors readable and test the effect in the browser.
Verify compatibility and accessibility when the feature or interface requires it.
